images.caption: Figure 1:Joints, Camera, Action! (JCA)generates a video and a synchronized 3D motion trajectory for a user-supplied rig of any topology. One model covers joint generation (top two rows) and either conditional direction (bottom two rows).Mesh animation:a rigged monkey clears a scene’s high-jump bar, adapting its motion to the surroundings.Keyframe control:given a first and last frame, JCA fills in the rig motion and video between them.Video-to-motion:recovering 3D motion from an input video.Motion-to-video:video following prescribed 3D motion.

Figure 2:Architecture overview.
Given a text prompt, a rig, and an optional reference image, the model jointly denoises video latentsZvZ_{v}and motion tokensZmZ_{m}. A graph network encodes the rig into per-joint descriptorsDD, using the joints’ 2D locations in the reference image, and these condition the motion branch; a graph-attention layer inside each Motion DiT block propagates features along the rig edges. Zero-initialized cross-attention bridges exchange features in both directions at paired blocks, each branch querying the other’s intermediate features, so joint training begins from the two pretrained branches acting as they did in isolation. An auxiliary joint-localization head (right) attends from joint features to video patches and returns each joint’s image position as a weighted combination of patch coordinates, giving 2D–3D correspondences used to fit a camera.

Figure 3:Text-driven rig animation across diverse assets. Each row shows a text prompt, an input mesh, and sampled poses from animations generated by competing methods and JCA (ours). Our method more faithfully captures the requested actions while preserving the asset’s geometry.

Figure 4:Additional Applications of our model.Top:Unlike the setting infig.1, we generate a video from a rig motion sequence and a text prompt, without an input image.Middle:An additional video-to-motion example with a different skeletal topology.Bottom:Given the rig and mesh of a real Unitree G1 robot, a 3D scene, an initial pose, and text, we jointly generate video and motion; we show the video alongside the mesh driven by the generated motion and rendered in the scene.

Figure 5:Scene-aware rig animation and motion localization. Given a penguin rig, a rendered initial frame of a snowy 3D scene, and a text prompt, our model jointly generates video and 3D rig motion.Top:frames from the generated video, where the penguin moves forward and slides down the snowy slope.Middle:the raw 3D motion produced by the motion branch, rendered in the input scene before localization. The penguin’s motion is not aligned with the depicted scene geometry and, in later frames, appears beneath the snow surface.Bottom:the same generated motion after applying our joint-localization and camera-alignment scheme described insection3.3. The estimated alignment correctly places the motion on the visible penguin and registers it with the generated video and scene.

Figure 6:Prompt-adherence evaluation of one animation with GPT-6 Astra. In the first turn, the judge is given the asset’s short description and 48 frames of the animation, 16 from each of the front, right, and left views, each frame labeled with its view; the figure shows two frames per view. It is asked to describe the motion it observes in chronological order. In the second turn, it scores the motion against the action prompt. The complete prompts and responses are given insectionB.3.
